title: Heaters, filters, lights and electrical safety
audience: Aquarium maintenance technicians who check or service heaters, filters, pumps, air pumps, lights and controllers
learningOutcomes: Identify the electrical hazards in aquarium heaters, pumps, filters, lights and controllers, and explain how water raises the risk
Isolate and check each item before any inspection or cleaning in the water area
Recognise a damaged heater, cord, plug or outlet, and take it out of service
Refer any wiring, repair, fixed lighting or controller work to a licensed person, without implying that this lesson grants any licence
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: NSW Government, Electrical licences and certificates (last updated 23 June 2026); Electrical Safety Office Queensland, Electricity around water (no date shown); Standards Australia, Wiring Rules (AS/NZS 3000:2018) (copyright 2026 in page footer; no revision date shown).

instruction.heading: Water and mains power
instruction.body: Aquarium heaters, pumps, lights, controllers and filters work in water or beside it, and they are powered from mains outlets. Water on a connection, a damaged cord or an unsuitable outlet can cause an electric shock or a fire. Common causes described in the sources include a heater running out of water, a cracked heater, a cord hanging into the water, and several devices on one double adaptor. Treat every aquarium electrical item as live until it has been unplugged or isolated, and check it before you use it.

instruction.heading: Heaters and thermostats
instruction.body: A heater must be fully submerged, or used only as the manufacturer directs, because a heater that runs out of water can overheat and crack. Check the heater for cracks, discolouration, loose parts and a damaged cord before it is used, and take a damaged heater out of service. Set the heater within the range the livestock plan gives (see the system types lesson). Keep a separate thermometer where it can be read easily, away from the heater, and compare the two readings at each visit. Do not repair a heater by taping or wrapping a damaged part. Replace it with a suitable unit, as the owner's plan and the product instructions direct.

instruction.heading: Filters, pumps and air
instruction.body: Filters and pumps need a clear intake and a working impeller. Check both for blockage before you reconnect the power, and never run a pump dry. A power filter that is opened or refilled must be full of water before it is plugged in. Check the flow at the outlet against the filter's rating on its label. Air pumps, air lines and air stones supply oxygen and circulation. Check the air line for kinks and leaks, and clean air stones as the manufacturer directs. A battery air pump is a useful backup in a power failure, and that choice belongs to the owner.

instruction.heading: Lights and timers
instruction.body: The light period is set by the owner's plan. Leaving the light on for long periods encourages algae, and a timer is commonly used to keep the period steady. The sources do not agree on the exact hours, so use the plan. Unplug a light before you remove it from the tank or clean it. Metal halide lamps run very hot, and a lamp must cool before it is handled, or be handled with gloves as the manufacturer directs. Bulbs are replaced at the manufacturer's interval.

instruction.heading: Cords, outlets and layout
instruction.body: Keep cords out of the water and away from splash zones. Make a drip loop, so that water runs down the cord and drips away rather than into the outlet. Do not use damaged cords, and do not use double adaptors that overload the outlet. Use one suitable power point, or a power board whose rating is checked against the load, and keep the outlet dry and above splash level where practical. Do not plug equipment into an outlet that is wet or looks damaged.

instruction.heading: Isolating before work
instruction.body: Unplug or isolate equipment before you remove it from the water, clean a filter, change media or check a connection. Check that the device is off before you put a hand in the tank. Wet hands, metal tools and water on the floor increase the risk, so dry your hands and keep the area dry. A safety switch, or residual current device, reduces the risk on the circuit, but it does not make live work safe and does not make the work allowed.

instruction.heading: Repairs and licensed work
instruction.body: Repairing or rewiring a mains connection, a controller or a fixed lighting installation is electrical work. In New South Wales, electrical wiring work, repairs included, needs a licence or certificate whatever its cost, except for electrical equipment operating at not more than 50 volts AC or 120 volts ripple-free DC (last updated 23 June 2026). A maintenance worker's role is to isolate, inspect the outside of the equipment, report the fault and refer it. Completing this lesson does not give electrical authority.

procedure: Isolate and unplug equipment before any handling in the water area.
Inspect each heater, pump, filter, air line, light, cord and outlet for damage, water on connections and loose parts.
Take any damaged item out of service, and label it.
Check that each heater is fully submerged, or set as the manufacturer directs, before it is switched on.
Check the cord layout and drip loops, and remove any double adaptor that overloads the outlet.
Refer any wiring, controller or fixed lighting fault to a licensed person, in writing.
Record the inspection, the items taken out of service and the referral.

workedExamples.situation: A heater in a small tank is cracked and has been running. The owner asks the technician to tape it so it can keep running until the weekend.
workedExamples.reasoning: A cracked heater is a shock and overheating hazard. The technician unplugs it, does not tape it, takes it out of service, labels it, and recommends a suitable replacement under the owner's plan. The cracked heater, the owner's request and the referral are recorded.

workedExamples.situation: A tank's filter cord hangs down the front of the tank, and there is a drip on the outlet.
workedExamples.reasoning: The technician isolates the outlet, creates a drip loop so that water runs off the cord, moves the cord away from the splash zone, checks the outlet for damage and dries it. If the outlet itself is damaged, the technician takes it out of use and refers the repair to a licensed person.

equipmentAndPpe: Drip loop cable ties or clips
Label or tag for equipment out of service

commonErrors.error: Running a heater out of water.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep the heater submerged as directed, and check the water level first.

commonErrors.error: Taping or wrapping a cracked heater or cord.
commonErrors.prevention: Take the item out of service and replace it.

commonErrors.error: Plugging several devices into one double adaptor.
commonErrors.prevention: Use suitable outlets, and do not overload them.

commonErrors.error: Working on a connection while it is still plugged in.
commonErrors.prevention: Unplug or isolate first, then prove the device is off.

commonErrors.error: Relying on a safety switch to make live work safe.
commonErrors.prevention: A safety switch reduces risk only. Isolate the equipment before work, and refer any live work.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Water and mains power together create a shock and fire risk. Isolate before handling, take damaged equipment out of service, and keep cords out of the water.

In New South Wales, electrical wiring work, repairs included, needs a licence or certificate whatever its cost, except for electrical equipment operating at not more than 50 volts AC or 120 volts ripple-free DC (last updated 23 June 2026). This lesson does not grant any licence.

The Queensland Electrical Safety Office page on electricity around water is written for pools. It recommends that electrical equipment be used through a safety switch and that cords and appliances be kept out of the water (no date shown).

AS/NZS 3000, known as the Wiring Rules, is the Standards Australia title for the technical guidance used when installations are designed and checked (copyright 2026 in the page footer; no revision date shown).

qualityStandard: Equipment is isolated before any handling in the water area
Damaged equipment is labelled and taken out of service
Each heater is confirmed submerged, or set as the manufacturer directs, before power is restored
Electrical faults are referred to a licensed person in writing
documentationEvidence: Items taken out of service, with label and date
Electrical referral with the fault description
summary: Treat aquarium electrical equipment as live until it has been unplugged or isolated.
Keep heaters submerged, cords out of the water, and use drip loops.
Take damaged heaters and cords out of service. Do not tape them.
Refer wiring, repair and fixed lighting to a licensed person, and remember this lesson grants no licence.

knowledgeChecks.question: An aquarium heater is cracked. What is the correct response?
options: Tape it and keep it running, since the crack is small and the heater still works
Run it at a lower setting, so the crack does not get worse over time
Unplug it, take it out of service, and recommend a suitable replacement
Leave it in the tank with the lid off so that the crack can cool down

knowledgeChecks.question: Why keep a cord out of the water and use a drip loop?
options: It stops water running down the cord into the outlet
It looks neater on the bench and in the tank room
It makes the pump quieter, which owners notice most
It changes the water temperature in the tank over time

knowledgeChecks.question: Who should repair or rewire a mains connection on an aquarium system?
options: Any technician who has time to look at the wiring this week
The owner, using a double adaptor to get the power to the heater
The livestock supplier, who knows the tank and its equipment best
A licensed person, as electrical work is licensed in many circumstances
